utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I understand you have some matters to raise before the witness comes in? Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for allowing me to raise this, Your Honour. Just briefly, I hope. I thought it might be helpful before the witness comes in to seek some clarification as to what the present procedural posture of the hearing that we're engaged in is. As you know, through a miscommunication, apparent miscommunication, Dr. de Man thought it was his brief to evaluate the fitness of Mr. Stanisic to stand trial. We proceeded to ask a number of questions yesterday concerning his report. The Chamber concluded yesterday's session by asking Dr. de Man the questions that are normally asked of experts regarding fitness. We have, of course, a decision of the Chamber find of Mr. Stanisic fit to stand trial. The Defence have not yet formally moved to reopen that issue and so I am just wondering where we are, and the reason that I am raising this is that if we either deliberately or inadvertently have reopened the issue of fitness, then the Prosecution is renewing its request to the Chamber to have Dr. Mimica see Mr. Stanisic again. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am not saying that we are reopening the decision, but it is perfectly clear to me that Dr. de Man's evidence raises questions which the Chamber felt obliged it to put to him the questions which we did put yesterday. Depending on how he answers those questions, and depending on the submissions that the parties make in relation to his evidence, the Chamber will determine what to do. It may very well include doing what you suggested. The Chamber's whole intention is to arrive at a decision which is proper and fair in all circumstances. So let the doctor be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, you will recall the questions that were put to you last evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I'd like to have a response from you in relation to those questions. The first question was: Is the accused able to understand the nature of the charges and proceedings against him including the consequences of a conviction on those charges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my answer to this question is yes. In my opinion, I do consider him able to understand these matters. My opinion is grounded in the fact that I did not find a significant disturbance of cognitive functioning on psychiatric examination. Also, Mr. Stanisic is oriented as to time, place, and person. However, I would like to note that his understanding is intact, as far as clearly cognitive understanding is concerned, more affective understanding, "verstehen" as in Jaspers, will be severely hampered by the accused's affective state, that is to say his depression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I missed the words which you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the presiding judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm saying that I missed the words which came after "more affective understanding."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's more affective understanding being the feelings behind the understanding and then I used the German word "verstehen" which is the part of the philosophy of psychiatrist philosopher Jaspers, Karl Jaspers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. So that's for the first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's for the first question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The second question: Is the accused able to instruct counsel as to his defence in relation to the charges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this question I answer in the negative. I do not consider him able to instruct counsel as to his defence. My opinion on this question is founded in my finding on psychiatric examination that the accused is severely distracted by a deeply depressed mood and depressive and suicidal ruminations, thereby lacking the necessary powers of concentration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And the third question: Is the accused able to testify on his own behalf if he has to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this question also I have to answer in the negative. In my opinion, the present state of the accused precludes him from being able to give evidence and to be cross-examined. The causes of this disturbance is the same as the reason for his being, in my opinion, unable to assist counsel, namely, my finding on psychiatric examination that the accused is severely distracted by a deeply depressed mood and depressive and suicidal ruminations thereby lacking the necessary powers of concentration. This finding is also at the basis of my classifying his actual level of functioning as reflected in his low score on the Global Assessment of Functioning scale we extensively discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In that low score, there was a reference to the judgement of the accused being affected. Would you like to comment on that in relation to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not very sure I understand what you want me to answer so -- or at least what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me find the table with the -- yes, you told Mr. Jordash that the principal basis for your conclusion that the accused was unfit was that you found his judgement impaired and you also found an inability, on his part, to function in almost all areas. I think those are two of the three factors mentioned in that category 21 to 30, and I wondered whether you would wish to elaborate on that in relation to the questions concerning whether he's able to testify on his own behalf and whether he's able to instruct counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I tried to put in my answer just now, but it may have condensed my answer a bit too much. One aspect is the depressed mood and the preoccupations with feelings of despair, hopelessness, and the depressive ruminations and suicidal thoughts which occupy his mind at the moment. And there is, so to speak, not much room for anything else. That is the reason why he is at this moment functioning at a very low level, and is also, in my opinion, not able to assist counsel in his own defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So not able to -- when you use the word assist, it's actually instruct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, instruct. I was a bit confused by the Dutch saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that. Now, the fourth question was whether the accused is physically able to withstand full-time trial proceedings, which is normally five days a week, five hours a day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in asking me that question, you put the term "physically" between parentheses, so I have done that in my answer also, and encompassed psychological functioning due to his mental state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just ignore the word "physically."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll ignore it for the moment. In my professional opinion, the accused, in his present state, is unable to withstand full-time proceedings. Even the mitigated schemes as proposed by the psychologist, Dr. Smit and by the psychiatrist, Dr. Mimica, would, in my opinion, not be possible. My opinion is based on my assessment of the severity of the depressive state which has gone from 21, meaning moderate on the 17-item Hamilton scale in the examination of Dr. Mimica on 29th of November, to 37, in my own examination of Mr. Stanisic on the 28th of March of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the last question is: Does his health situation require any particular accommodation to support his ability to stand trial? It's very much related to the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In my opinion, I -- what is required at the moment is adequate clinical care including vigorous psychiatric treatment. At the moment of examination, treatment of this nature and quality was offered by the UNDU medical staff including the psychiatrist, Dr. Vera Petrovic, and by the staff of the penitentiary hospital. Further decisions on treatment policy need, in my opinion, to be made on the basis of experience gained in this particular case and depending on further developments in the case. In my experience, and to my knowledge, full restoration of functioning is well within the realm of possibility in a case like this, despite the severity of the depression at its present stage, and the presence of psychotic features.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us go back to question number four, whether he's able to withstand full-time trial proceedings. You said that he wouldn't be able to withstand even the mitigated schemes proposed earlier by other doctors. I'm not sure exactly what you are saying. Are you saying he can't withstand any trial proceedings or whether he's to be tried four days a week or three days a week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was what Dr. Mimica advised that he should be tried only one part of the day and three days a week, but at this moment, I think he will be not only be able to function in a trial which is for the -- which was answered in the first questions, but also that the trial as such would be deleterious to him at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to come back to you. So in plain terms, what are you saying? In plain terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is not only -- he is, at this moment, simply too sick to be here. To say it in normal words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have one or two questions to ask you. You stated yesterday that your report was made on the basis of an examination of Mr. Stanisic at one particular point in time. In fact, you saw Mr. Stanisic for an examination which lasted less than one hour or one hour, approximately. You were well assisted by an interpreter. He was hospitalised. He had had morphine administered to him and he was apparently suffering from renal problems at the time. Do you think that your conclusions regarding the mental state or health of Mr. Stanisic are nevertheless relevant if he is not hospitalised, if he doesn't have any physical problems, if he does not take morphine anymore, et cetera, et cetera? In other words, is your conclusion, according to which you're stating that he is not capable of withstanding trial because of his mental state, but would these conclusions still be applicable today while he is no longer in a hospital or would that still be applicable in a week from now, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason I -- the reasons I gave for my judgement of the mental state of Mr. Stanisic are due to psychological condition, first and foremost, because I am not an expert on his -- on his gastrointestinal or other physical ailments. Nevertheless, I do agree with you that his physical state and his mental state are clearly linked and that the story of Mr. Stanisic in the recent past, as he told me in his experience of suffering blows, both physically and mentally during the last month, are intermingled. Nevertheless, the depth of his depression was very clear to me at the time of examination, which would have lasted longer if the clinical conditions of Mr. Stanisic had permitted me to do. And this finding, the severity of the depression is the foundation of my advice to the Court. I hope my answer is satisfactory to Your Honour. Not really?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I believe that you've answered in part, certainly, my question. I think that it is clear that Mr. Stanisic is suffering from a deep depression, and I believe that every doctor that examined him would agree on that point, and agree on that point, for that matter. But the question I would like to put to you is to -- is the following: You said that his depression deteriorated, in other words, it became even deeper lately but you only met him on one occasion so this is a conclusion that you drew from probably what Dr. Petrovic told you or what Mr. Stanisic told you himself. But I'm wondering if his depression became more severe because of his physical problems when you examined him or if, in fact, he is more or less in the same state, approximately a month ago when he was examined by other physicians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My conclusions from studying his file on record within the detention unit was that the development in the recent period has been a negative one, and besides the sayings of Dr. Petrovic, I have based that impression both on written data within his medical charts and on Dr. Paulus Falke with whom I also spoke in this matter. Especially that was in fact the only question I asked from him is: How do you see the development? And he agreed with Dr. Petrovic that there was a rapid deterioration taking place. Sorry about that word. I do agree with you that -- and that's the reason why I mentioned that in my -- the answer to the Learned Judge's last question being that we have to follow-up on the examinations made in the past which, as you, in my opinion, rightly said do show a great deal of common ground besides having a certain difference within the severity of the depression. There's no discussion about the diagnosis, apart from the psychotic features, but the -- the fact that there is a depression is acknowledged only we see a falling off of the severity. Yet it gets worse, not lighter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge David has a question but I just wanted to see whether I could clarify for the doctor what I believe Judge Picard was asking him. I think the substance of her question is whether the doctor believes that the fact that the accused had been administered morphine some time before, perhaps shortly before the examination, and that he had hallucinations caused by mirtazapine, whether these factors accounted for the condition in which you found him and therefore, explained your finding so that absent those, let us call them, external factors, would you have found the accused in the same condition to warrant the finding that you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Thank you very much for this clarification, Judge. One of the points is that I am not convinced that the hallucinations which have been reported in several cases by Mr. Stanisic for a long period of time stem from the mirtazapine, although I -- of course I cannot prove that they don't, but the time-frame does give me the opinion that the nightly occurrences which Mr. Stanisic reports are -- do predate his use of mirtazapine. As to the morphine, I specifically asked Nurse Remelsvan [phoen] to instruct me as to the time when he did get morphine and she told me that that was in the evening before his examination which means about 18 hours before, and he did not get a repeat dosage. That is what I was told. So due to the half-life of the drug, I did not judge his clinical situation to be significantly altered by the fact that he had been treated with morphine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Dr. de Man, in the previous reports of the experts Mimica and Smit, they say that it was possible that a depression was a reaction to his incarceration. And this has been reflected in paragraph 75 of our Chamber's decision. Do you believe that depression, in the psychiatric and psychological literature as well as in this case is an accompanying factor to most incarcerated persons, especially when the prospects are for long-term incarceration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prospect of long-term incarceration is something which is maybe unfortunately quite known to be, as I have been working in long-term prisons, and what -- we do see changes in behaviour due to long-term incarceration, but clinical depression even amongst people incarcerated for a long time while threatened by a life sentence or even having been sentenced to life imprisonment is still quite rare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: The report I have in front of me indicated that in epidemiological studies done both in the U.S. and Canada, psychiatric syndromes, severe depression is part of the evolutionary process of people when they feel themselves with the prospect of dying in prison or long-term possibilities of staying there. Do you believe that in the case of Mr. Stanisic, the increased level of depression is caused by the prospect of his own "verstehen," if you want, of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the prospect of severe sentence being given and prolonging of what he experienced -- experiences as being banished from his own country is certainly a very severe burden and contributive factor to the clinical state of Mr. Stanisic, there's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: So it might follow that it is a precipitating factor in the aggravation or it could be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could very well be. It certainly is contributive to the total image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: If that is so, there is no, then, alternatives to every inmate in the same situation except alleviation through psychological and biological therapy or physiological therapy, you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that people incarcerated are entitled to the same kind of care people outside get. I'm sure that this Tribunal has the same opinion. But that is not the same as opening the back door, I can understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: You said yesterday, if I am not mistaken, that this is a dynamic process.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: It is not an irreversible process, neither an instructural condition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If the parties have questions to put to the doctor, they may do so. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Doctor, I just have a couple of questions based on the answers that you've given. There are two topics that I want to cover. One is the process by which Mr. Stanisic should be evaluated, what you think is the optimal process, and the other question is about the care that is available, as you know it, in the United Nations Detention Unit. To begin with the first question or the first topic, excuse me. Yesterday, when describing the way that this process would go forward in the criminal justice system of the Netherlands, you used words such as longitudinal, and multi-disciplinary, and today, you have said that it would require experience with Mr. Stanisic and "further developments in the case."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The question is this: Could you describe to us how a situation like this, how a defendant like Mr. Stanisic, charged with a serious crime, stating that he is psychiatrically unfit to stand trial, how would that be evaluated in the Netherlands criminal justice system?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you something about that. What we try to do within the Netherlands penitentiary system is to have adequate care available, even to those who are -- have to stay within the confines of the prison system. For that, we have Statute law which makes it possible to treat people while they are still legally incarcerated, either within a hospital or within TBS facility, which is a special facility, special hospital which is under the regulations of the Dutch government. That means that we don't have to lose control, you might say, our Prosecutors don't have to lose control of a detainee once complicated treatments are necessary. That's one aspect. The other aspect is -- and that's maybe something your learned friend from the Defence might instruct you about from his scientific point of view. Our view, the Dutch view of being -- of unfitness to stand trial has a much higher threshold than in the Anglo-Saxon system or in Germany, for example, where unfitness to stand trial and the ability to assist counsel is weighed much more heavily than in the Dutch legal system. But I'm afraid it's very difficult to make a good comparison between the two systems in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I was unclear. I understand that treatment would be available, even in a penal setting within the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But my question was more if an accused, if a criminal, a person charged with a crime says, "I am not able to be tried," how is that claim able to be evaluated? And the reason I'm asking that question, and don't let me put words in your mouth, but I have picked up in several of the answers you have given, some dissatisfaction with the limits on your ability to talk with Mr. Stanisic. You wanted to see him at different times. You wanted to see him for more time. So I'm wondering how would that be handled in the Dutch system.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Dutch system, an important question like that would be addressed by at least two specialists working together. One of them -- always a forensic psychiatrist, and the second almost always a clinical or mental health psychologist or -- appointed court experts. In some cases, there is a third-party evaluation by psychiatric social worker but that's mostly just in case of a first trial and not in a case like this. There is a third possibility which is admission to a special remand house we have in Utrecht called Pieter Baan Centrum where extensive multi-disciplinary observation by psychologists, psychiatrists and psychiatric social workers is possible, and that examination would last for seven weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I was going to ask how long the Pieter Baan Centrum evaluation would last but you've answered that. Would it be fair to say that you would want to see Mr. Stanisic over a longer period of time and on more occasions than you have been able to do so far?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: About how much longer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be very beneficial to be able to see him. We generally do two or three times and a third or fourth time in order to explain the results to be examined because that is one of the things we are bound to do. The duration of the -- each examination will be dependent on the clinical state, so it may be that we see somebody for four times, two hours, but in the case of Mr. Stanisic, we would tend, as long as he is in a bad state as I saw him on the 28th, I wouldn't want to see him longer than this hour, because of the principle of not harming the examined person. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And how long would pass if you saw him, let's say, four times, how much time would pass between examinations to the extent that it's possible to answer such a question?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, when I get an order from the Dutch courts, they give me eight weeks in order to prepare my report, in which time I have to examine the subject, but also have to confer with my colleague, and because mostly it's a multi-disciplinary evaluation, and sometimes it's also necessary to ask for help in formulating our advice clear enough for the court and then we can use special lawyers who are part of the organisation of NIFP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: By NIFP, that's the Netherlands Institute for Forensic Psychology?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. And that's both the organisation which -- which is responsible for treatment within the prison system and for advice to peripheral courts is part of that organisation, but also Pieter Baan Centrum is one of the working units of NIFP.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What sorts of cases are evaluated at the Pieter Baan Centrum versus evaluated on the sort of schedule that you have just outlined for us?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one legal obligation of Pieter Baan Centrum is to see people who are under a remand order because you need an incarceration in order to be able to put somebody under observation within the prison system. And besides that, we try to limit the admission to Pieter Baan Centrum, which of course has a limited capacity, to severe cases in which the decision has a great effect on the decision of the court -- advice has the great effect on the decision of the court as it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What in your view, are the advantages of an evaluation of the sort that you have been outlining in your answers to the last few questions that I have put to you as opposed to a single visit such as you have had with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course a single visit would be exceptional even in ordinary cases, because we always try to see people two or three times, but the order of the Court was clear that I had to examine him on the 28th and deliver a report on the 1st of April which didn't give much -- any space, I must say. I understand -- I quite understand that given the circumstances, but in ideal circumstances, for a clinical evaluation, we would -- we would like to use more time and the advantage of -- I checked with your question for a moment, if you don't mind -- the advantage of extensive clinical examination is that you can -- you get more opportunity, so to say, to second-guess yourself. You're not only with several disciplines but you can go back at any moment and check on a certain point. You have the observation of skilled personnel who also see somebody on a 24 and 24 basis in a small group of six or eight people being under observation. You get all kinds of data which you put together to a report from the Pieter Baan Centrum is generally about 50 to 60 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The second topic I wanted to cover, I wanted to clear up something from yesterday, and I confess I did not entirely catch this as you were saying it. But were you told anything on the 28th of March about Dr. Petrovic's availability over the preceding month? It sounded to me like you said that she had been in Belgrade and thinking about it, I wasn't clear how long she had been in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I had heard was that she was back in the Netherlands for the last for, I think, one or two weeks before my examination. And before that, she had been in Belgrade for two or three weeks, I'm not sure how long because I'm not familiar with her exact schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you know if Dr. Petrovic is not available because she is in Belgrade or for any other reason, are any -- is any psychotherapy available in the UNDU other than the continued administration of prescribed anti-depressant medications?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, unlike the other experts, we got Dr. de Man's answers to these questions just today so may I have a moment to consult with Mr. Groome before concluding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just two final questions, Doctor, and then I will be finished. When you say that when you say that at the Pieter Baan Centrum a patient is under 24 out of 24-hour observation and therefore you get lots of data, what sort of data do you get? What are these observations oriented towards, what is the point of these observations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is to observe the symptoms of the person under observation over a long period of time, that means also that they are objectified. Of course you do gather a lot of trivia is this way. So reading a report from the Pieter Baan Centrum can sometimes be an exercise in data mining but that does not mean it's not a good system. You do get -- you can get information you discard later on but it gives you much more security about the persistence of symptoms over time, whether they can be objectified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And lastly, in your opinion, how often should Mr. Stanisic be seen in order to do an evaluation that is not hampered by the limitations you have described on the evaluation you have been able to do?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to make a proper examination, being unable to answer questions as to the kind of treatment, for example, which should be offered and the effects of the incarceration, I think I would need at least three or four visits and be able to confer with colleagues on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How often, in your view, should Mr. Stanisic be seen by a psychotherapist for treatment, or how frequently, at what rate?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a difficult question to answer because as I already said in my last answer, that the scope of my evaluation was not such that I can give well-founded advice as to treatment. So I think I will have to give -- not to give you an answer on this question, because I simply haven't evaluated the accused significantly to be able to give you that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Understanding that, Doctor, nevertheless, could Dr. Petrovic's absence have been a contributing factor to the observed severity of Mr. Stanisic's symptoms which you found on the 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot exclude the fact, but I have no positive indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should have said that the court deputy informed me that the accused was at the detention unit. He had been informed that the doctor indicated that he was not well enough to attend court and that the customary documentation will be provided to the Chamber and I want to stress to the court deputy the importance of that documentation being sent to the Tribunal as quickly as possible. May I ask whether Mr. Knoops has any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Dr. de Man, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You testified, Doctor, that I quote: "I was only able to examine Mr. Stanisic for one hour and the clinical conditions had permitted me not to see him longer." Now, would you agree that this hour visit was due to his medical condition, i.e., the level of exhaustion or lack of concentration that you had to break-up your visit after one hour?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was clearly too tired for me to continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You were also asked by the Learned Judges about the potential influence of the factor incarceration on the GAF scale?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you agree that the GAF score is an overall score and therefore, the level of incarceration as such is only one of the many factors you accounted for?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Now, speaking about the -- actually the moment of depression and the fact whether there is a relationship or not with the incarceration, I noticed in your report on page 3 that you spoke with the accused about the moment his condition deteriorated. It's on page 3, second paragraph. You mentioned, "On the subject of his cooperation with counsel."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: "Mr. Stanisic states that he has been able to work with the Defence team very well until 7 or 8 months ago as his condition deteriorated." Now, my question to you is, Doctor, whether you were able to find any positive indications in your evaluation of this case, the data you saw, that the deterioration in terms of his clinical depression indeed started before his incarceration?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I checked this with Dr. Petrovic, whether I understood well what Mr. Stanisic had told me. I did come to the conclusion that the moment of decline was, in fact, during his stay in Serbia Montenegro, not during the incarceration time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Now, as to treatment and the possibility of restoration of his situation, as you clearly indicated that it's not irreparable, would you say that as a professional, such a restoration of mental state, preferably should take place in a clinical environment instead of a detention environment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a clinical point of view, a detention environment is not something you would prescribe. Nevertheless, it is my experience as a forensic psychiatrist also working in a prison system from 1988 that good clinical care on -- that you might say on an out-patient basis, can be offered within the prison system and even with serious depressions, I see that both in my official practice and in my private practice at home, that it is possible to treatment severely ill people outside of the clinic. The decision whether somebody has to be admitted to a psychiatric hospital or to a facility like we have within the Dutch prison system, that decision is a multi-factorial one. You cannot -- it's not a one-on-one relationship between the severity of the illness and the necessity of clinical hospitalisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But you would agree that as a professional, if you had to prescribe any form of treatment, you would give your preference to a situation whereby the patient is in a clinical environment instead of a detention environment.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would try and have the same -- well, same is difficult, but almost the same reason for admission inside or outside the -- my -- the point I judge when asked whether somebody is fit to be detained, which is something which is much more frequent question asked by Dutch courts, "detentie geschiktheid" they call that, then I usually say that nobody is fit to be detained from a psychiatric point of view but that once the necessary medical treatment turns out to be impossible within the prison system, then there is a compelling need to hospitalise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Doctor, you were asked some questions by my learned friend of the Prosecution about the Pieter Baan Centrum, the observation clinic who operates under the auspices of the ministry of justice in the Netherlands. Would you agree with me that the Pieter Baan Centrum is not a -- an institution for mental recovery but rather to arrive at a proper diagnosis of an accused person? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would entirely agree with that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And would you agree with us that we have a diagnosis, not only from you, but also from other experts. Therefore, the focus of the future of this case should be the proper treatment instead of considering the accused to be admitted to the Pieter Baan Centrum where primarily, the diagnosis has to be made.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the diagnosis, the prognosis on treatment is of course part and parcel of a full clinical observation which also can take place at the Pieter Baan Centrum. It's not a treatment centre. But they do give advice on the treatment necessary, both within the TBS system and outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Speaking about the prospect of the recovery of Mr. Stanisic, and the Court's decision on the basis of your testimony, would you agree with Dr. Falke's position as explained in his letter of 17 March 2008. I will just quote --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please, I'm not familiar with that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm quoting from Dr. Falke's letter, second letter of Dr. Falke of 17 March 2008, last paragraph. "With regard to point 3 in the court order, further expert examinations are contraindicated at this point from a medical point of view, as they can further increase the anxiety of the patient and can act as a catalyst to the depression."

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you agree with the observation of Dr. Falke that any further examinations by other experts could indeed result in this phenomenon as described by Dr. Falke?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it is always a risk that an examination, so to speak, stirs up the mud in a person's psychological make-up which could make for a worsening of his situation. That was the reason why I limited my examination to this one hour, because I, primum non nocere, try at least not to do harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And, Doctor, if you would confine yourself to the case at hand, would you agree that this risk as described by Dr. Falke is realistic in the case of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a risk of an examination overdose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Two final questions, Doctor. You also questioned about the -- and you mentioned yourself the follow-up examinations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you agree that any follow-up examinations should be conducted instead of in terms of weeks, in terms of months in light of your prognosis that the deep depression could only recover at the least between six -- at least between three and six months?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your question. What I meant to say in seeing -- in the mentioning that the further decisions on treatment policy need to be made on the basis of experience based on follow-up, there is also the follow-up of treating physicians who should have restoration of functioning on their agenda. So it's not just the examination of independent experts, of course, which are a necessary evil, in this case, but also the examination by treating physicians and their report either to the independent experts or to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. My final question is: Doctor, you have answered the questions of the Learned Judges, the five additional questions, do you expect that your answers to those five questions will change within the three months from now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to that question, Your Honour. That's highly speculative and the witness should not be expected to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness, in my view, is in a position to answer it and to provide a basis other than speculation, if he can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm always afraid of being speculative, I must say. The change in the condition of Mr. Stanisic which forms the basis of my answers I already stated in my first report that I expected some time, three to six months, to be necessary in order to recover from this depression which has lasted for more than -- for about a year now, and is -- has become more severe. This is on the basis of what I know of the general pattern of recovery from depression. I cannot predict, and I would not like to predict exactly what may happen, but if, from a statistical point of view, and you know statistics always lie when you have one person in front of you, but from a statistical point of view, I would expect this three months to be reasonable. But I cannot predict the -- what is going to happen within the next few months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And Doctor, to be completely clear, that's -- that prospect you just described is a prospect which is conditioned upon proper treatment, i.e., psychotherapy on a structural basis?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH DE MAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is based on an effective treatment of the depression and the latest insights are that both talking and medication are necessary for -- to achieve a cure in this matter. And of course the total environment is of the utmost importance also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, sir, I would like to ask an additional question. What would be the time-frame regarding the potential cure of the patient? You've just answered that question, but what the Court is interested in would be what period of time would be necessary in order for him to be fit to be judged? To be fit for court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid that's one of the answers you can only be -- we can only find on follow-up, because if somebody does get better, he doesn't get better in the same pattern, and you should -- we should also take into consideration the fact that an early return to the box might even mean that the recovery is hampered. Nobody knows that at the moment. You have to follow that very closely during treatment itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, I just wanted to clarify something that you have testified about more than once, that is the deterioration in the condition of the accused. The last time that he was seen by one of the doctors who testified before us was the end of February, that's February 29th, and you examined him on the 28th of March. That is exactly a month. Are you satisfied that the kind and level of deterioration that you saw could take place in the space of 28 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that is possible, especially in view of the fact that there also were medication changes in those -- in this period of time, and his physical condition did undergo some changes also, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doctor, that concludes your evidence, and the Chamber is grateful for you to coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will now hear submissions from the parties on their assessment of the evidence of the doctor, and -- Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have received a good deal of information in the last hour and 15 minutes. It would be a help to the Prosecution in giving the Chamber a succinct and well-organised submission if we could take the recess a bit early and counsel could consult before making their submissions, if the Court please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I wasn't asking to adjourn for the day, I was just asking for the usual 20-minute break earlier than usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We knew you were more industrious than that, Mr. Docherty. I should say that what I want you to concentrate on in your submissions is what impact if any has Dr. de Man's evidence made on the Chamber's finding of fitness. That, to my mind, is the crucial issue. We will adjourn then for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On the question posed by the Chamber, the effect of Dr. de Man's report on the Chamber's previous finding that the accused Jovica Stanisic was fit to stand trial, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not just his report but also the evidence that he gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The Prosecution notes that the Chamber's earlier decision was based on a thorough analysis of reports and testimony from a number of mental health professionals. We also note that Dr. de Man was quite clear both in his evidence today and in his report that he found no cognitive impairment in Mr. Stanisic. Dr. de Man saw Mr. Stanisic one time for less than 60 minutes, although he was granted access to the medical file, he was not able to look at it until later. And at the time that he met with Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Stanisic was suffering from renal colic and 18 hours earlier had been administered morphine. Even under these circumstances, Dr. de Man found no cognitive impairment and of course, the Strugar opinion requires that there be a cognitive impairment of some sort or other before an accused can be found psychiatrically unfit to stand trial. It is therefore the Prosecution's position that Dr. de Man's report and evidence do not unseat this Chamber's earlier decision, and the Prosecution therefore recommends that once Mr. Stanisic is physically fit for trial, which we understand from the medical reports should be later this week or early next week, the trial should commence. This should be coupled with continued psychotherapy and with regular psychiatric reports from the treating psychiatrist about Mr. Stanisic's progress. In the Chamber's decision of the 10th of March, 2007, it was ordered that, "The Trial Chamber will receive a report on the medical condition of the accused once a week from the resident doctor of the UNDU so as to allow for adjustments in the schedule to be made where necessary. In addition, the accused is to be examined at least once every four weeks or more often when necessary by a gastroenterologist." The Prosecution would request that this be extended to a regular report from the treating psychiatrist with, of course, the necessary and I hope obvious proviso that progress report be given without going into the content of any therapeutic conversations. In other words, Your Honour, a strict application of the strict letter of the law would say that we should go forward with this trial. We recognise, of course, that the report and the evidence of Dr. de Man could be a cause of concern. And contrary to what my learned friend Mr. Knoops said in a question that he put to Dr. de Man, there is not, at this point, if Dr. de Man's report is taken at its face, there is not at this point agreement on a diagnosis. There is agreement on a general level of diagnosis which is to say that Mr. Stanisic is depressed. But there is no agreement on the cause of that depression. Is it a reaction to incarceration? To family issues? Is it a matter of biochemistry? Is it a reaction to his physical ailments? Is it a combination of these? There is no agreement on the severity of his depression. The hallucinations reported by Dr. de Man are self-reported by Mr. Stanisic, and even Dr. de Man can't rule out the possibility that mirtazapine, which he has been taking for the last month, is a cause of those hallucinations. And there is no agreement on treatment. If you look at Dr. de Man's report, there is an enumeration there of a number of different drugs that have been tried with Mr. Stanisic over a period of time. Taking into account the concern that Dr. de Man's report and testimony may have caused, the Prosecution persists in its recommendation that the trial should commence, but offers as an alternative recommendation that Mr. Stanisic be evaluated within the Dutch criminal justice system as outlined today by Dr. de Man. And in particular, we would recommend that Mr. Stanisic go to the Pieter Baan Centrum in Utrecht for observation. There, 24-hour observation, as Dr. de Man indicated, would be possible. This will take into account the very real possibility of malingering which, after a preliminary review of the literature, is a genuine and serious concern in cases such as this one. There will be no more self-reporting of symptoms but rather, as Dr. de Man said, symptoms will be objectified, will be studied, will be observed by outsiders. There will be a detailed report submitted to the Court. We have had very preliminary consultations with the Netherlands authorities and it appears on the basis of those preliminary discussions, that Mr. Stanisic could be evaluated in the Dutch system. We would further ask if the Court decides to go down this particular path, that Dr. Mimica also see and evaluate Mr. Stanisic once again. The advantages of that are that Dr. Mimica has seen Mr. Stanisic in the past and has done a forensic evaluation of him. That Dr. Mimica speaks the language of the accused, and shares with the accused a common culture. For all of those reasons, Your Honour, the Prosecution submits both its primary and its secondary, if you will, assessment or recommendation, excuse me. The primary being that the trial should go forward because there has been no finding of a cognitive impairment. The secondary being that there should be a thorough evaluation, not a one-time visit by Dr. de Man, upon which the Chamber can base future decisions as to the course of this trial. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Docherty. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, it's the primarily argument of the Defence that seen from the best interests of the accused, we, in this stage at this point will not argue reopening of the fitness issue as such. Rather, we would like indeed to comment on the impact of the evidence Dr. de Man gave yesterday and today on Your Honour's decision of the 10th of March and its consequences for the continuation of the case. I have three topics to address to Your Honours. First, of course, the impact of his evidence on the decision of the 10th of March. Secondly, the issue of the foundation of his evidence and the evidence as such. And in the third place, I will conclude with certain concluding observations and especially in view of the five options Your Honours presented to the Prosecution and Defence last week. As to the first topic of my submissions today is when we would look into the impact of the evidence of Dr. de Man upon the ratio decidendi of Your Honours's decision we would actually detect five elements. First, his evidence is simply new forensic evidence. It's dealing with a new forensic situation. It's evidence that is new simply because Your Honours' decision is stemming from the 10th of March. We are now almost a month further and despite the therapy or the treating the accused is undergoing in the detention centre, there is not any improvement, rather, there is a significant deterioration, to use the words of Dr. de Man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying that the mere fact of the time difference in the examination constitutes a new element?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We are not at liberty to comment on that, Your Honour, as being not experts. We can also submit that it will take more time than expected for any recovery of the accused persons. The evidence given by Dr. de Man is to be taken very serious because, in our humble submission, it's the best evidence the Chamber has received until yesterday. It's evidence issued by a renowned neuropsychiatrist and above that, it's evidence given by a court-appointed expert. An expert who was, in our submission, fully informed and knowledgeable. There is, in our submission, no room for doubt as to the credibility of the testimony given by Dr. de Man. Now, speaking in specific about the impact of his evidence on Your Honours' decision of the 10th of March, we submit that there are two major elements to be detected in his evidence. First, the deterioration in terms of the depression as evidence by the objective standards used by Dr. de Man with respect to the GAF scale, has an impact, we believe, on the paragraphs 76 and 77 of Your Honours' decision where Your Honours relied upon the evidence given by Dr. Mimica. As to the new evidence presented by Dr. de Man, by the way, concurred by Dr. Petrovic as evidenced by his statement, is clearly the forensically new element of psychosis, of psychotic features which impacts upon the paragraphs 39 and 130 of Your Honours' ruling of the 10th of March where Your Honours presupposed absence of any psychotic disorders or features. In the third place, the evidence of Dr. de Man has a clear impact upon Your Honours' ruling in specific on paragraph 131 of your decision where Your Honours assumed that a modified trial schedule would accommodate the potential disabilities of the accused person. And we believe that the evidence of Dr. de Man given yesterday and today has also an impact on the five options Your Honour has presented to the Defence and Prosecution of last week. Based on this new forensic evidence given by this expert, he also arrives at one crucial new element for Your Honours in comparison with the decision of the 10th of March, this clearly relates to the answering of the five fitness questions. Dr. de Man has answered the first question and therefore, deviates from the other experts who based themselves on the previous situation of the accused in medical terms. The answer to his first question is that Mr. Stanisic's understanding is intact. We're dealing now with the first question of the fitness issue, yet a more effective understanding - Dr. de Man used the German word "verstehen" - will be severely hampered by his mental and medical state. This is clearly something new which was not before the Chamber when it ruled on the 10th of March. This is clearly something new based on the changing in the situation. Also when overviewing the answers of Dr. de Man with respect to the remaining four fitness questions, one can say that forensically, the Court deals with a new situation. I noted with respect to the fourth question that even with mitigating schedules, it is not possible for the accused to attend proceedings or to participate due to the severity of his depressive state. Lastly, Your Honours, speaking about the impact upon your decision of the 10th of March. I would like to refer to Your Honours' ruling or holding in the paragraphs 50 and 51 of the decision of the 10th of March where Your Honours have held that, "Trying an unfit accused has been compared to trying an accused in absentia." We believe that virtually we are dealing now with that situation and this is clearly something new and clearly has and should have, in our humble submission, an impact upon the decision of the 10th of March. Now, my second topic deals shortly with the foundation and the evidence as such of Dr. de Man. As mentioned, Dr. de Man is a highly qualified neuropsychiatrist affiliated with the Dutch Ministry of Justice. Above that, his view concurred on all areas with the view of the treating psychiatrist, Dr. Vera Petrovic and of Dr. Falke. Dr. de Man used the data and the available reports, at least he was fully informed when he gave evidence to this Court by reading the previous reports and I recall that Dr. de Man said that he was fully acquainted with the assessment of Dr. Mimica and that to a certain extent, he agreed with Dr. Mimica yet while the situation changed, he could come to a different conclusion as opposed to that of Dr. Mimica. So we are not dealing with an expert as suggested by my learned friend from the Prosecution who had initially, of course, only access to the reports, didn't read them, but when given his evidence before Your Honours yesterday and today, he was fully informed about those data. Now, as to the one-hour examination by Dr. de Man, we should keep in mind that this one hour was limited due to the situation, the medical situation of the accused, which clearly is an indication of the severity of the situation as opposed to an apparent lack of thoroughness of his evidence. And in that respect, we should keep in mind, with all due respect, that also Dr. Mimica saw Mr. Stanisic only once in October 2007. When we look into the evidence as such, Your Honour, the evidence presented by Dr. de Man to Your Honours yesterday and today, it's highly persuasive. It leaves no room for doubt, in our submissions. It clearly shows that it is possible that such a significant deterioration, even on the GAF scale can take place within one month, and I believe it was the Learned Judge, presiding Judge Robinson who just asked the expert about the question whether it is possible that in one month, the health condition of the accused can deteriorate, and I believe the answer of the expert was clearly in the affirmative. I think the evidence also clearly indicates that any suggestion that this depression might be contributed to any fault on the part of the accused is that he is not willing to take medication or he is reluctant to take medication has now been actually counterbalanced by the evidence of Dr. de Man. It is not something which has to do with the position of the accused as to taking medication, it has to do with the proper treatment as such. And we believe that when it concerns the exact cause of this severe depression, the Prosecution again refers to the private situation of the accused. Of course this is one of the factors which may have led to the situation, but we are not dealing now any more with the exact causes, we're dealing with the fait accompli that we are dealing with an accused person who, in our submission, is not able to participate in his proceedings. Your Honours, looking further at the evidence of Dr. de Man, it is clear that the expert was again in full agreement with Dr. Petrovic, also including the rapid deterioration that was on questions of the Learned Judge Picard and that Dr. de Man answered that question. And also the potential argument that his assessment was due to the morphine, I think was counterbalanced by the remark of Dr. de Man that the morphine was adduced to the accused 18 hours before his examination, therefore the results and the assessment by Dr. de Man had clearly nothing to do with the morphine and the situation as a result thereof. What is particularly striking, Your Honours, is that Dr. de Man used objective tests to come to the conclusion that indeed there was a severe deterioration. When you look into the report of Dr. Mimica on page 15, you find the GAF scale on 65 until 70 while we're dealing now with the GAF scale of 21 to 30 and a Hamilton rating scale on page 13, Dr. Mimica reports related to 21 while Dr. de Man referred to 37, which, in his view, is a clear indication of a severe depression, telling the Court that 37 is, "As far as one can get." Of course the evidence cannot be assessed without going into the credibility of Dr. de Man's evaluation. In that respect, it is notable, Your Honour, that the presence or absence of any psychotic features was not part of the rating scale that Dr. de Man testified. Even without the reported hallucinations, Dr. de Man would remain within the GAF scale of 21 until 30 was his testimony, and above that, the accused met all three descriptions on the GAF scale: Exhaustion, fears lower his functioning, he testified. When speaking about the GAF scale and the principal cause for the daytime impairment, which is clearly forensically a new situation the Court is dealing with, Dr. de Man testified that these are related to factors, "Other than the reported hallucinations." Most importantly, Dr. de Man testified that the previous reports upon which Dr. Mimica reported did not change his opinion. Dr. de Man was quite familiar with the evidence given by the other expert, in particular, Dr. Mimica, and he specifically referred to Dr. Mimica's report by saying that it didn't change his opinion. As to the fitness itself, Dr. de Man testified that there is a very strong change in severity between his assessment and the previous reports. Your Honour, I now conclude with my observations for the Chamber. At this point, we submit that there is ample reason, legally and also forensically to grant an adjournment of the trial proceedings for at least three to six months. At this moment, there is ample evidence before the Court that trial proceedings can, in all reasonableness, not take place as they would de facto tantamount to a trial in absentia, see the paragraphs 50 and 51 of the Your Honours' decision of the 10th of March. Dr. de Man testified on questions of the Honourable Judge David that it is possible that the illness of Mr. Stanisic is treatable, it's not irreversible was his testimony. Therefore, in light of the case law we discussed last week, invited by the Chamber on the five options, we believe that this is a viable and also reasonable alternative instead of proceeding with the case including the option which was suggested to proceed through a videolink participation. If one thing has learned us today and yesterday, it is that even that option, in view of the evidence before the Chamber, is absolutely not realistic. Lastly, Your Honour, what we learned today from Dr. de Man's evidence is that any further examination through a potential renewal of the fitness issue and/or inviting other experts to assess the condition of Mr. Stanisic can be contra-indicative and even function as a catalyst for the well being of Mr. Stanisic as written by Dr. Falke in his letter of 17 March which was affirmed today by Dr. de Man's testimony. Therefore, we believe that the suggestion of the Prosecution to consider having Mr. Stanisic being detained in the Pieter Baan Centrum, the Dutch forensic observation clinic, would be against the best interests of the accused and could further hamper his health situation, apart from the fact that Dr. de Man confirmed that the Pieter Baan Centrum observation clinic is primarily there to arrive at a proper diagnosis for the Dutch courts to see whether they can proceed with a case. It's not a treating clinic, as such. This was also confirmed by Dr. de Man's evidence today. And therefore, while all experts in this case are in agreement that Mr. Stanisic suffers from a depression, however they differ as to the nature and the severity thereof, we don't believe, we submit, that a detainment in the Pieter Baan Centrum clinic would be favourable to, and would assist the Court in finding a proper solution for the trial proceedings. In conclusion, we believe that based on this persuasive testimony of Dr. de Man of yesterday and today, notably by court-appointed expert, based upon the principle of best evidence, the Court should not follow the suggestions of the Prosecution to continue with this case, should not continue -- should not consider a treatment or detention in the Pieter Baan Centrum clinic but instead could ask Dr. de Man if the Court would follow the second option as suggested by the Defence, namely an adjournment for at least three months, could ask Dr. de Man to inform the Court in a time-frame as set by the Chamber. To inform the Court about any development in the medical situation of Mr. Stanisic. Further examination by any other expert, and that might also include Dr. de Man, as we know now, might be contra-indicative for the situation of the accused. These are our submissions and therefore, we respectfully request the Court to follow the second option as argued last week by the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In giving its decision on this issue, the Chamber does so on the well-known standard for reconsideration of a Chamber's decision in the Tribunal, and that standard is that a Trial Chamber's decision will be reconsidered in exceptional cases if a clear error of reasoning has been demonstrated or if it is necessary to do so to prevent an injustice. The Chamber, by majority, Judge Robinson dissenting, decides that having read the report of Dr. de Man, having heard his evidence, and having heard the submissions of the parties, there is no need to reconsider its decision as to the accused's fitness. The Chamber will adjourn now for 20 minutes and return to give instructions as to the future course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided that the decision on the future course of the trial will be given in writing, and that decision will be available tomorrow for the parties. That decision will indicate when the trial will begin. In those circumstances, we are adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.35 p.m.
